column1: Why does Financial Management aim to maximise shareholder wealth rather than profit?
column2: Profit ignores timing, risk and cash reality; wealth (market value of equity) captures time value, risk and long-run cash flows — profit can be inflated yet destroy value.

column1: Why is Wealth Maximisation superior to Profit Maximisation as the goal of FM?
column2: It uses cash flows (not accounting profit), accounts for time value of money and risk, and reflects the true owner benefit — share price.

column1: What are the three key decisions of Financial Management?
column2: Investment (capital budgeting), Financing (capital structure), and Dividend decision — each affects value and risk.

column1: Why does time value of money exist even without inflation?
column2: A rupee today can be invested to earn a return, so it is worth more than the same rupee later — opportunity cost of waiting.

column1: Why do we discount future cash flows instead of adding them directly?
column2: Future rupees are not comparable to present rupees; discounting converts them to a common time-point so value is measured correctly.

column1: What is the Future Value formula for a single sum?
column2: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n — compounding a present sum forward at rate r for n periods.

column1: What is the Present Value formula for a single sum?
column2: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n — discounting a future sum back at rate r.

column1: Why is an annuity due worth more than an ordinary annuity of the same amount?
column2: Cash flows arrive one period earlier, so each is discounted for one less period — PV(due) = PV(ordinary) x (1 + r).

column1: What is the PV of a perpetuity?
column2: PV = Cash flow / r — a constant flow forever, value equals flow divided by discount rate.

column1: What is the PV of a growing perpetuity?
column2: PV = C1 / (r - g), valid only when r > g — used in the Gordon dividend model.

column1: Why must r be greater than g in the growing perpetuity formula?
column2: If g >= r the series does not converge; value would be infinite/negative, which is meaningless.

column1: What does NPV represent and what is the decision rule?
column2: NPV = PV of inflows - PV of outflows; accept if NPV > 0 because the project adds value above the required return.

column1: Why is NPV theoretically the best capital budgeting technique?
column2: It uses all cash flows, time value, correct discount rate, and gives value added in absolute rupee terms — directly linked to wealth maximisation.

column1: What is IRR and its accept/reject rule?
column2: IRR is the rate where NPV = 0; accept if IRR > cost of capital (hurdle rate).

column1: Why can IRR mislead for mutually exclusive projects?
column2: It ignores scale and assumes reinvestment at IRR; NPV (reinvestment at cost of capital) is more reliable — prefer NPV on conflict.

column1: Why can a project have multiple IRRs?
column2: Non-conventional cash flows (more than one sign change) produce more than one root — use NPV or MIRR instead.

column1: What does the Profitability Index (PI) measure and its rule?
column2: PI = PV of inflows / initial investment; accept if PI > 1 — useful to rank projects under capital rationing.

column1: What is the Payback Period and its main weakness?
column2: Time to recover the initial outlay; weakness — ignores time value and all cash flows after payback.

column1: How does Discounted Payback improve on simple payback?
column2: It uses discounted cash flows so time value is respected, but it still ignores flows beyond the payback point.

column1: Why do we add back depreciation when computing project cash flows?
column2: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; it was deducted for tax but does not leave the firm — cash flow = PAT + depreciation.

column1: What is the depreciation tax shield?
column2: Depreciation x tax rate — the tax saved because depreciation is deductible, a real cash inflow even though non-cash.

column1: Why are sunk costs excluded from capital budgeting?
column2: They are already incurred and unaffected by the decision; only incremental future cash flows are relevant.

column1: Why must opportunity cost be included in project evaluation?
column2: Using a resource in this project forgoes its next-best cash benefit; that lost benefit is a real economic cost.

column1: Why is interest expense excluded from project operating cash flows?
column2: Financing cost is captured in the discount rate (WACC); including it in cash flows double-counts the cost of capital.

column1: What is the Cost of Capital and why is it the discount rate?
column2: It is the minimum return investors require; a project must beat it to add value, so it is the hurdle for discounting.

column1: What is the formula for cost of equity under the Dividend Growth (Gordon) model?
column2: Ke = (D1 / P0) + g — dividend yield plus growth rate.

column1: What is the cost of equity under CAPM?
column2: Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf) — risk-free rate plus beta times market risk premium.

column1: Why is the cost of debt taken after tax?
column2: Interest is tax-deductible, so the effective cost = I x (1 - t); the tax shield lowers the real burden.

column1: What is WACC and why weight by market value?
column2: WACC = weighted average of component costs; market-value weights reflect the current opportunity cost investors face, unlike book values.

column1: Why is retained earnings not a free source of capital?
column2: Shareholders forgo dividends they could reinvest; its cost equals the cost of equity (often minus flotation) — an opportunity cost.

column1: What is Financial Leverage and what does it measure?
column2: % change in EPS / % change in EBIT (= EBIT / (EBIT - I - Pref/(1-t))); sensitivity of EPS to EBIT from fixed financial costs.

column1: What is Operating Leverage and what does it measure?
column2: % change in EBIT / % change in sales (= Contribution / EBIT); sensitivity of EBIT to sales from fixed operating costs.

column1: What is Combined Leverage and what does it capture?
column2: DCL = DOL x DFL = Contribution / (EBIT - I); total sensitivity of EPS to a change in sales — overall business + financial risk.

column1: Why does high financial leverage raise risk to equity holders?
column2: Fixed interest must be paid regardless of EBIT; in bad years EPS falls faster and insolvency risk rises.

column1: What is the indifference point in EBIT-EPS analysis?
column2: The EBIT level where EPS is equal under two financing plans; above it debt gives higher EPS, below it equity is safer.

column1: What does the Net Income (NI) approach say about capital structure?
column2: More debt (cheaper) lowers WACC and raises firm value continuously — an optimal structure is 100% debt (unrealistic assumption).

column1: What does the Net Operating Income (NOI) approach say?
column2: WACC and firm value are constant regardless of leverage; cheaper debt is exactly offset by rising cost of equity — no optimal structure.

column1: What is the core conclusion of Modigliani-Miller without taxes?
column2: Capital structure is irrelevant; firm value depends on operating earnings and risk, not on how it is financed (arbitrage enforces this).

column1: How does MM change when corporate taxes are introduced?
column2: Value of levered firm = value of unlevered + (tax rate x debt); the interest tax shield makes debt add value.

column1: What is the Traditional approach to capital structure?
column2: A moderate use of debt lowers WACC to a minimum and maximises value; beyond an optimal point, rising risk raises WACC again.

column1: Why does Trade-off theory say firms do not use 100% debt despite tax shields?
column2: Rising bankruptcy and financial-distress costs eventually offset tax benefits; the optimum balances tax shield against distress cost.

column1: What does Pecking Order theory predict about financing choice?
column2: Firms prefer internal funds first, then debt, then equity last — driven by information asymmetry and signalling costs.

column1: What is Working Capital and the two concepts of it?
column2: Capital for day-to-day operations; Gross WC = total current assets, Net WC = current assets - current liabilities.

column1: Why does an aggressive working capital policy raise both risk and return?
column2: It uses more short-term (cheaper) finance and low liquidity — lower cost boosts return but raises liquidity/refinancing risk.

column1: What is the Operating Cycle?
column2: Time from buying raw material to collecting cash from sales = inventory period + debtors period - creditors period.

column1: Why does a longer operating cycle increase working capital needs?
column2: More cash is tied up in inventory and receivables for longer before cash returns, so more funding is required.

column1: What is the formula for the Cash (Net Operating) Cycle?
column2: Inventory days + Receivables days - Payables days — the net time cash is locked in operations.

column1: What does the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) minimise?
column2: Total inventory cost = ordering cost + carrying cost; EOQ is the order size where these two are balanced/minimised.

column1: What is the EOQ formula?
column2: EOQ = square root of (2 x annual demand x order cost / carrying cost per unit) — the cost-minimising order quantity.

column1: Why does ordering more per order lower ordering cost but raise carrying cost?
column2: Fewer orders cut ordering expense, but larger average stock raises storage/capital carrying cost — EOQ trades them off.

column1: What is the purpose of a Cash Budget?
column2: To forecast cash inflows/outflows so the firm can plan for surpluses (invest) and shortfalls (arrange finance) in advance.

column1: What do the Baumol and Miller-Orr models optimise?
column2: Optimal cash balance — Baumol assumes steady cash use; Miller-Orr sets upper/lower control limits for uncertain cash flows.

column1: Why offer a cash discount for early payment of receivables?
column2: To speed collection and cut the debtors period; accept only if discount cost < benefit of reduced investment and bad debts.

column1: What is Factoring of receivables?
column2: Selling debtors to a factor for immediate cash (minus fee); transfers collection and sometimes credit risk (non-recourse).

column1: Why value closing stock at lower of cost or NRV?
column2: Prudence — never carry an asset above realisable cash; recognise a probable loss now but never an unrealised gain.

column1: What does a high Current Ratio potentially signal negatively?
column2: Excess idle current assets — overstocking or slow collection — hurting profitability despite strong liquidity.

column1: Why is the Quick (Acid-test) Ratio stricter than the Current Ratio?
column2: It excludes inventory (least liquid current asset), testing ability to pay short-term dues from near-cash assets only.

column1: What does Return on Equity (ROE) measure?
column2: PAT available to equity / shareholders' funds — profit generated per rupee of owners' capital.

column1: How does DuPont analysis decompose ROE?
column2: ROE = Net Profit Margin x Asset Turnover x Equity Multiplier — profitability, efficiency and leverage drivers.

column1: What does the Debt-Equity ratio indicate?
column2: Financial leverage/solvency — proportion of debt to equity; higher means more fixed obligations and risk.

column1: What does Interest Coverage Ratio measure?
column2: EBIT / Interest — how many times operating profit covers interest; higher means safer debt servicing.

column1: Why can two firms with equal profit have very different ROE?
column2: Different leverage and asset efficiency; the equity multiplier and turnover reshape how profit translates to owner return.

column1: What is the Walter model's core idea on dividends?
column2: When r > Ke retain all (growth firm, payout 0); when r < Ke pay all out; when r = Ke payout is irrelevant.

column1: What is the Gordon model's bird-in-hand argument?
column2: Investors prefer certain current dividends to uncertain future gains; higher payout can raise value when r < Ke.

column1: Why is MM dividend irrelevance true under perfect markets?
column2: Investors can create homemade dividends by selling shares; with no taxes/costs, payout policy cannot change wealth.

column1: Why is a bonus issue not a source of cash for the firm?
column2: It capitalises reserves into shares; no cash enters — shareholders get more shares of the same total value.

column1: What is Business Risk versus Financial Risk?
column2: Business risk arises from operations (sales/cost variability, operating leverage); financial risk arises from using fixed-cost debt.

column1: Why does diversification reduce risk in a portfolio?
column2: Imperfectly correlated assets' movements partly offset; unsystematic risk is diversified away, lowering total variability.

column1: What is systematic (market) risk and can it be diversified?
column2: Risk from economy-wide factors (interest, inflation, recession); it is non-diversifiable and measured by beta.

column1: What does beta measure in CAPM?
column2: Sensitivity of a security's return to market return; beta > 1 more volatile than market, < 1 less volatile.

column1: What is the Security Market Line (SML)?
column2: The CAPM line plotting required return against beta; assets above it are underpriced, below it overpriced.

column1: Why does the Strategic Management process start with vision and mission?
column2: They set the long-term direction and purpose, giving a reference point against which all strategies and goals are judged.

column1: What is the difference between Vision and Mission?
column2: Vision is the aspirational future state (where we want to be); Mission is the present purpose and reason the firm exists.

column1: What are the components of a SWOT analysis?
column2: Strengths and Weaknesses (internal) plus Opportunities and Threats (external) — matches internal capability to external environment.

column1: What is the purpose of PESTLE analysis?
column2: Scan the macro-environment — Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental factors that shape opportunities and threats.

column1: What are Porter's Five Forces?
column2: Threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, power of suppliers, threat of substitutes, and rivalry among competitors.

column1: Why do Porter's Five Forces determine industry profitability?
column2: They set the intensity of competition and who captures value; strong forces squeeze margins, weak forces allow high profits.

column1: What are Porter's three Generic Strategies?
column2: Cost Leadership, Differentiation, and Focus (cost-focus or differentiation-focus on a narrow segment).

column1: Why is being 'stuck in the middle' dangerous per Porter?
column2: A firm neither lowest-cost nor clearly differentiated has no competitive edge and loses to focused rivals on both sides.

column1: What does Porter's Value Chain analyse?
column2: Primary and support activities that create value; managing linkages and margins builds competitive advantage.

column1: What are the primary activities in Porter's Value Chain?
column2: Inbound logistics, Operations, Outbound logistics, Marketing & Sales, and Service.

column1: What are the support activities in Porter's Value Chain?
column2: Firm infrastructure, HR management, Technology development, and Procurement.

column1: What does the BCG Growth-Share Matrix classify?
column2: Business units by market growth and relative market share: Stars, Cash Cows, Question Marks, and Dogs.

column1: What is the recommended strategy for a BCG 'Cash Cow'?
column2: Harvest — low growth, high share; milk steady cash to fund Stars and Question Marks with minimal investment.

column1: What should a firm do with a BCG 'Question Mark'?
column2: Selectively invest to build share into a Star, or divest if it cannot gain position — it consumes cash with uncertain payoff.

column1: What are the four strategies in Ansoff's Product-Market Matrix?
column2: Market Penetration, Market Development, Product Development, and Diversification.

column1: Which Ansoff strategy carries the highest risk and why?
column2: Diversification — new product in a new market means the firm lacks both product and market experience.

column1: What is the difference between Related and Unrelated diversification?
column2: Related shares synergies (technology, market, channels); unrelated (conglomerate) enters wholly different businesses to spread risk.

column1: What is the GE Nine-Cell (McKinsey) Matrix?
column2: Positions units on industry attractiveness vs business strength (3x3) to decide invest/grow, selectivity, or harvest/divest.

column1: What is the difference between Strategy Formulation and Implementation?
column2: Formulation is deciding what to do (analysis, choice); implementation is doing it — allocating resources, structure, and execution.

column1: What are the three levels of strategy in an organisation?
column2: Corporate (which businesses), Business (how to compete in each), and Functional (operational support for the strategy).

column1: Why must structure follow strategy (Chandler)?
column2: The chosen strategy dictates the coordination and resources needed; the organisational structure must be designed to deliver it.

column1: What is Strategic Control?
column2: Monitoring and adjusting strategy as it unfolds using premise, implementation, surveillance and special-alert control.

column1: What is a Core Competence (Prahalad and Hamel)?
column2: A unique capability that provides customer value, is hard to imitate, and gives access to many markets — basis of advantage.

column1: What does Turnaround strategy address?
column2: Reversing a declining business — cost cutting, asset reduction, revenue generation and focus to restore viability.

column1: What is the difference between Expansion and Retrenchment strategy?
column2: Expansion grows scope/scale (new products/markets); retrenchment reduces it (divest, liquidate, turnaround) to cut losses.

column1: What is a Strategic Business Unit (SBU)?
column2: A self-contained division with its own market, competitors and profit responsibility, managed as a distinct planning unit.

column1: Why is competitive advantage sustainable only if hard to imitate?
column2: If rivals can copy it cheaply, the advantage and its extra profit erode quickly; barriers/uniqueness make it durable.

column1: What does a Balanced Scorecard measure beyond finance?
column2: Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, and Learning & Growth perspectives — linking strategy to operational metrics.

column1: Why does strategic management emphasise the external environment?
column2: Firms are open systems; survival depends on adapting to opportunities and threats they do not control, not just internal strengths.
